items.text: Vertical vs horizontal scaling: scaling up buys a bigger box with a hard ceiling and a single point of failure; scaling out adds machines but forces you to handle partitioning and coordination.
Stateless services scale horizontally because any instance can serve any request. Push session state to a shared store (Redis, a DB) or into a signed token.
Amdahl's law: if 10% of a workload is serial, no number of parallel workers can make it more than 10x faster.
Little's law: concurrency = throughput x latency. At 1,000 req/s and 200 ms latency, about 200 requests are in flight at any moment.
Autoscaling lag: new instances take minutes to boot and warm up, so scale on leading signals (queue depth, CPU trend) and keep headroom for sudden spikes.
Utilization vs latency: queueing delay explodes near saturation. In an M/M/1 queue at 90% utilization, requests wait about 9x the service time before being served.
Cell-based architecture: split the fleet into independent cells that each serve a slice of customers, so a bad deploy or poison request only hurts one cell.
L4 vs L7 load balancing: L4 routes by IP and port, fast and protocol-agnostic; L7 parses HTTP, so it can route by path, header or cookie and terminate TLS.
Round robin assumes all requests cost the same; least-connections adapts much better when request durations vary widely.
Power of two choices: pick two random backends and send the request to the less loaded one. It nearly matches global least-loaded without any global state.
Sticky sessions pin a user to one backend. They simplify stateful apps but create hot spots, and users lose their session when that node dies.
Health checks: active checks probe endpoints on a timer; passive checks eject backends after real request errors. Using both catches crashes and gray failures.
DNS load balancing is cheap but coarse: clients and resolvers cache records, sometimes beyond the TTL, so DNS-based failover can take minutes.
Anycast: the same IP is announced from many locations and BGP routes each user to the nearest one. CDNs and DNS providers use it for latency and DDoS absorption.
Cache-aside (lazy loading): the app checks the cache, and on a miss reads the DB and fills the cache. Simple and resilient, but first reads are slow and data can go stale.
Write-through cache: every write updates cache and DB synchronously. Reads stay fresh, but writes get slower and the cache fills with data nobody reads.
Write-back (write-behind) cache: writes land in the cache and flush to the DB asynchronously. Very fast writes, but a cache crash before the flush loses data.
Write-around cache: writes go straight to the DB, skipping the cache. Avoids polluting it with write-once data, but the next read of that key is a guaranteed miss.
Invalidate by deleting the cache key on update rather than setting the new value; racing writers that set values can leave the older one in the cache.
Cache stampede (thundering herd): a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the DB at once. Fix it with a per-key lock or single-flight so only one caller recomputes.
TTL jitter: add random spread to expirations (e.g., 300 s +/- 10%) so keys cached at the same moment don't all expire, and miss, at the same moment.
Stale-while-revalidate: serve the expired value immediately and refresh it in the background, trading a moment of staleness for steady latency.
LRU eviction drops the least recently used item. Great for recency-heavy workloads, but a single large scan can flush the entire hot set.
LFU eviction drops the least frequently used item. It keeps long-term favorites, but needs aging or decay so once-hot keys don't squat forever.
Negative caching: briefly cache 'not found' results, or bugs and attackers querying nonexistent keys will bypass the cache and hammer the database.
Hot key problem: one key with huge traffic overloads the single cache shard that owns it. Replicate it across shards or add a small in-process cache in front.
Cache hit ratio math: going from 90% to 99% hits cuts database load 10x, because misses fall from 10% to 1% of requests.
HTTP caching: Cache-Control max-age sets freshness; an ETag with If-None-Match lets clients revalidate and receive a tiny 304 Not Modified instead of the full body.
CDN: edge servers near users serve static and cacheable content, cutting latency and origin load; the origin only sees cache misses.
Push vs pull CDN: push uploads content ahead of time (good for large, rarely changing files); pull fetches from origin on the first miss (simpler, first user pays).
Cache busting: put a content hash in asset filenames (app.3f9a1c.js) so files can be cached forever and a deploy takes effect instantly via new URLs.
Origin shield: a mid-tier CDN cache in front of the origin collapses misses from many edge POPs into a single origin request.
B-tree index: turns an O(n) full table scan into an O(log n) lookup, and supports range queries and ORDER BY because keys are kept sorted.
Every index speeds up some reads but slows every write, because each INSERT or UPDATE must also maintain all indexes on that table.
Composite index on (a, b, c) serves filters on a, a+b, or a+b+c, but not on b alone. This is the leftmost-prefix rule.
Covering index: when the index holds every column a query needs, the database answers from the index alone without touching table rows.
Random UUIDv4 primary keys scatter inserts across a B-tree, causing page splits and cache misses; time-ordered IDs (UUIDv7, ULID, Snowflake) append at the right edge.
Connection pooling: DB connections are expensive (Postgres forks a process per connection), so a pool of a few dozen busy connections beats thousands of idle ones.
Replication lag: async replicas are usually milliseconds behind but can fall minutes behind under heavy writes or long queries. Monitor lag and pull slow replicas from rotation.
Sync vs async replication: sync waits for a replica ack (no data loss on failover, higher latency); async returns at once (fast, but recent writes can vanish on failover).
Hash vs range sharding: hashing spreads load evenly but sends range queries to every shard; range sharding keeps ranges local but risks hot shards on sequential keys.
Shard key choice is nearly permanent: pick a key with high cardinality, even distribution, and presence in most queries, or every query becomes scatter-gather.
Celebrity problem: sharding by user_id puts all of a celebrity's traffic on one shard. Split hot entities further or give them special handling.
Cross-shard joins and transactions are expensive. Co-locate related data (e.g., all of a tenant's rows on one shard) so most queries touch a single shard.
Resharding trick: pre-split into many logical shards (e.g., 4096) mapped onto fewer physical nodes, so growth means moving whole logical shards, not rehashing keys.
SQL vs NoSQL: relational DBs give joins, constraints and multi-row ACID transactions; many NoSQL stores trade those for easier horizontal scaling and flexible schemas.
Isolation levels: Read Committed prevents dirty reads, Repeatable Read also prevents non-repeatable reads, and Serializable prevents all anomalies, including write skew.
Write skew: two doctors each check that someone else is on call, then both go off call. Snapshot isolation allows it; serializable isolation or explicit locks prevent it.
MVCC: readers see a consistent snapshot while writers create new row versions, so reads never block writes. Old versions need garbage collection, like Postgres VACUUM.
Optimistic locking: keep a version column and run UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = N. If zero rows change, someone else won; reload and retry.
Write-ahead log (WAL): changes are appended and fsynced to a log before data pages are modified, so after a crash the database recovers by replaying the log.
CQRS: separate the write model from one or more read models so each can be optimized independently; read models are usually eventually consistent.
Event sourcing: store every state change as an immutable event and derive current state by replaying them. Full audit history, but harder queries and schema evolution.
Online schema migration uses expand/contract: add the new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, and only then drop the old column in a later deploy.
Change Data Capture (CDC): tail the database's replication log (e.g., Debezium reading the Postgres WAL) to stream row changes to caches, search and warehouses.
Queue vs pub/sub: a queue delivers each message to one consumer (work distribution); pub/sub delivers each message to every subscriber (broadcast).
Queue-based load leveling: producers keep writing at peak while consumers drain at a steady rate, so bursts become backlog instead of outages.
Visibility timeout (SQS): a received message is hidden, not deleted. If the consumer doesn't delete it before the timeout, it reappears for another consumer.
Dead letter queue: after N failed deliveries, move the message aside so one poison message can't block the queue or loop forever.
Kafka vs RabbitMQ: Kafka is a replayable, partitioned log where consumers track their own offsets; RabbitMQ is a broker that routes messages and deletes them once acked.
Ordering is usually per partition, not global. To keep one user's events in order, use user_id as the partition key.
Consumer parallelism in a partitioned log is capped by partition count: a topic with 12 partitions supports at most 12 active consumers in one group.
Batching: sending 100 messages per request amortizes network round trips and fsyncs, trading a few milliseconds of latency for a large throughput gain.
Stream windows: tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping, sliding windows overlap, and session windows close after a gap of inactivity.
Event time vs processing time: events arrive late and out of order, so stream processors use watermarks to decide when a time window is complete.
Claim-check pattern: keep messages small by storing large payloads in blob storage and sending only a reference through the queue.
Token bucket: tokens refill at rate r up to capacity b, and each request spends one. It allows bursts of up to b while enforcing an average rate of r.
Leaky bucket: requests enter a queue that drains at a fixed rate, smoothing bursts into steady output; when the queue is full, excess requests are dropped.
Fixed window counter: count requests per clock minute. Cheap, but a client can send 2x the limit by bursting at the end of one window and the start of the next.
Sliding window log: store a timestamp per request and count those within the last window. Exact, but memory grows with the request rate.
Sliding window counter: estimate with two counters, e.g., current + previous x (fraction of previous window still overlapping). Nearly exact at constant memory.
Distributed rate limiting: a central Redis counter updated atomically (INCR or a Lua script) is accurate but adds a hop; per-node local limits are faster but approximate.
Rate limit responses: return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header so well-behaved clients back off instead of hammering.
Rate limit by the right key: per-IP limits punish users behind shared NAT; per API key or user is fairer, with per-IP kept as a coarse abuse layer.
Idempotency keys: the client sends a unique key with a POST; the server stores the result under that key and returns it on retries, so a retried payment charges once.
An idempotency key must be recorded atomically with the operation's effect; if a crash can happen between them, a retry can still execute twice.
HTTP semantics: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by spec; POST and PATCH are not, which is why POST needs idempotency keys for safe retries.
Offset pagination (LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000) slows down on deep pages because the DB still walks the skipped rows, and inserts shift items between pages.
Cursor (keyset) pagination: WHERE id > :last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 jumps straight to the page via the index and stays stable while rows are inserted.
API versioning: URL versions (/v2/) are explicit and cache-friendly; header versions keep URLs clean. Either way, additive changes shouldn't need a new version.
REST vs gRPC: REST with JSON is universal and easy to debug; gRPC uses HTTP/2 and Protobuf for compact, typed, streaming calls, and shines between internal services.
GraphQL lets clients fetch exactly the fields they need in one call, but moves complexity to the server: query cost limits, N+1 resolvers, and harder HTTP caching.
Long polling vs SSE vs WebSockets: long polling is simple but chatty, SSE streams server-to-client over plain HTTP, and WebSockets give full-duplex messaging.
Webhooks: sign payloads with HMAC, include an event ID so receivers can dedupe, and retry with backoff, because receivers will sometimes be down.
ETag + If-Match gives optimistic concurrency over HTTP: an update fails with 412 Precondition Failed if someone else changed the resource first.
SLI vs SLO vs SLA: the SLI is the measured metric (success rate), the SLO is the internal target (99.9%), and the SLA is the contractual promise, set looser than the SLO.
Error budget: a 99.9% SLO allows 0.1% failure, about 43 minutes of downtime per 30 days. When the budget is spent, slow releases and fix reliability.
Nines of availability per year: 99% is ~3.65 days of downtime, 99.9% ~8.8 hours, 99.99% ~53 minutes, and 99.999% ~5.3 minutes.
Serial dependencies multiply availability: three services at 99.9% each, called in a chain, give about 99.7% end to end.
Redundancy adds nines: two independent replicas at 99% each give 1 - 0.01^2 = 99.99%, but only if their failures are truly independent, which they rarely are.
RED method for services: Rate (requests/s), Errors (failed requests/s) and Duration (latency distribution). A solid default dashboard for every endpoint.
USE method for resources: Utilization, Saturation and Errors for each CPU, disk, NIC and memory. Saturation (queueing) often shows trouble before utilization hits 100%.
Report latency as percentiles, not averages: a 50 ms mean can hide a 2 s p99 that one in every hundred requests experiences.
You can't average percentiles across hosts. Merge histograms or sketches (HDR histogram, t-digest) and compute percentiles from the combined data.
Distributed tracing: a trace ID propagated through every hop (the W3C traceparent header) stitches spans into one request tree that shows where time is spent.
Trace sampling: head-based sampling decides at the start (cheap, but misses rare errors); tail-based decides after completion, so slow or failed traces can be kept.
High cardinality kills metrics: a label like user_id creates one time series per user. Keep IDs in logs and traces, not in metric labels.
Alert on symptoms, not causes: page when users are hurting (SLO burn, error rate), not when CPU hits 80%, which may be perfectly harmless.
Burn-rate alerting: page when the error budget burns at about 14x the sustainable rate over an hour, catching real outages fast while ignoring brief blips.
Circuit breaker: after failures cross a threshold, stop calling the dependency (open) and fail fast; after a cooldown, let a trial request through (half-open) to test recovery.
Bulkhead: give each dependency its own thread or connection pool, so one slow dependency can't exhaust the capacity that every other call needs.
Exponential backoff with jitter: wait random(0, base x 2^attempt) between retries so clients that failed together don't retry in synchronized waves.
Retry amplification: if each of 3 layers makes up to 3 attempts, one failing call can become 27 attempts at the bottom. Retry at one layer only.
Retry budgets: allow retries only up to about 10% of normal request volume, so retries smooth over blips but can't multiply load during an outage.
Only retry failures that may succeed later: timeouts, 503s and connection resets. Don't retry 4xx errors, and never retry non-idempotent calls without idempotency keys.
Every network call needs a timeout. Without one, a hung dependency slowly ties up every thread and connection, and the caller goes down with it.
Deadline propagation: pass the remaining time budget downstream (as gRPC deadlines do) so services stop working on requests the caller has already given up on.
Backpressure: when a consumer can't keep up, signal producers to slow down (bounded queues, TCP flow control, reactive streams) instead of buffering without limit.
Load shedding: when overloaded, reject excess requests early and cheaply (e.g., a fast 503) so the requests you do accept still finish within their deadlines.
Graceful degradation: when a dependency fails, serve a reduced experience (cached recommendations, hide the reviews widget) instead of failing the whole page.
Metastable failure: a brief trigger causes retries or cache misses that keep the system overloaded after the trigger is gone. Shedding load breaks the feedback loop.
Liveness probes should only confirm the process is alive. If liveness checks the database, one DB blip makes the orchestrator restart every pod at once.
Canary deploys: send a new version 1% of traffic first and compare its error rate and latency against the baseline before rolling out to everyone.
RPO vs RTO: RPO is how much data you can afford to lose (time since last good copy); RTO is how long recovery may take. Together they drive backup and failover design.
Multi-AZ vs multi-region: AZs in a region are linked with low latency, so sync replication is practical; regions are far apart, so cross-region replication is usually async.
Latency numbers: L1 cache ~1 ns, main memory ~100 ns, SSD random read ~16-100 us, same-datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms, cross-continent round trip ~150 ms.
A day has 86,400 seconds; round it to 10^5 for estimates. One million requests per day is only about 12 requests per second on average.
Size for peak, not average: peak traffic is often 2-10x the daily average due to daily cycles, launches and events.
Storage estimate: 100M new records/day x 1 KB = 100 GB/day, about 36 TB/year; with 3x replication, roughly 110 TB/year.
Random vs sequential I/O: an HDD seek costs ~10 ms, so a spinning disk does only ~100-200 random reads/s while streaming 100+ MB/s sequentially.
Bandwidth estimate: 1 Gbps is about 125 MB/s. Serving 1 MB images at 10,000 req/s needs roughly 80 Gbps of egress.
QPS from DAU: 10M daily users x 10 requests each / 86,400 s is about 1,200 req/s average; plan for peaks of 2-3x that or more.
Object storage (S3, GCS): flat key namespace, effectively unlimited capacity and very high durability, but higher latency than block storage and no in-place edits.
Store large files in object storage and keep only metadata and the object key in the database; blobs bloat DB backups, replication and memory.
Pre-signed URLs let clients upload or download directly to object storage with time-limited permission, keeping big transfers off your app servers.
Multipart upload: split large files into parts uploaded in parallel and retried individually. S3 caps a single PUT at 5 GB, so bigger objects require it.
LSM tree: writes go to an in-memory memtable, flush to immutable sorted SSTables, and are merged by background compaction. Excellent write throughput.
LSM reads may check the memtable and several SSTables; per-SSTable Bloom filters let them skip files that definitely don't contain the key.
B-tree vs LSM: B-trees update pages in place and give predictable reads; LSMs turn writes into sequential appends, favoring write-heavy loads at the cost of compaction.
Write amplification: one logical write can cause many physical writes (B-tree page rewrites, LSM compaction), hurting throughput and SSD lifetime.
Bloom filter: a compact bit array that answers 'definitely not present' or 'maybe present'. No false negatives; about 10 bits per key gives ~1% false positives.
Erasure coding: store data as k data chunks plus m parity chunks (e.g., 10+4) to survive m losses at ~1.4x overhead, versus 3x for triple replication.
Columnar storage (Parquet, ClickHouse) stores each column contiguously, so analytics reading a few columns over billions of rows scan far less and compress well.
Inverted index: maps each term to the list of documents containing it, so a search intersects posting lists instead of scanning every document.
Text analysis (tokenizing, lowercasing, stemming 'running' to 'run') must match at index time and query time, or searches silently miss documents.
BM25 ranking: scores documents by term frequency with saturation, inverse document frequency (rare terms count more) and document length normalization.
Elasticsearch fixes an index's primary shard count at creation; changing it means reindexing or using split/shrink, so size shards from expected data volume.
Typeahead: precompute the top-k completions for each prefix (in a trie or prefix table) and cache them, since each keystroke has a ~100 ms latency budget.
Geospatial search: geohashes or quadtrees turn 2D locations into prefixes; query the user's cell plus its 8 neighbors to catch points near cell edges.
Hash passwords with a slow, salted algorithm (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2), never a plain fast hash like SHA-256. Salts defeat rainbow tables; slowness defeats brute force.
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. Check authorization server-side on every request, not just by hiding buttons in the UI.
JWTs are verifiable without a DB lookup, but can't be revoked before expiry without a denylist. Keep access tokens short-lived and pair them with refresh tokens.
OAuth 2.0 is for delegated authorization (access tokens); OpenID Connect adds an ID token on top of it for authentication.
SQL injection: always use parameterized queries. Concatenating user input into SQL lets attackers rewrite the query itself.
TLS provides encryption, integrity and server authentication; mutual TLS also authenticates the client, a common basis for zero-trust service-to-service traffic.
Envelope encryption: data keys encrypt the data, and a master key in a KMS encrypts the data keys, so rotating the master key doesn't mean re-encrypting all data.
CSRF: browsers attach cookies to cross-site requests automatically. Defend with SameSite cookies and anti-CSRF tokens on state-changing requests.
XSS: escape untrusted output for its context (HTML, attribute, JS) and set a Content-Security-Policy so injected scripts can't run.
URL shortener: 7 base62 characters give 62^7, about 3.5 trillion codes, enough for billions of links with room to spare.
URL shortener codes: base62-encoding a unique counter avoids collisions entirely; hashing the URL needs collision checks. Hand out ID ranges per node to avoid a bottleneck.
URL shortener redirects: a 301 is cached by browsers (less load, but you lose click analytics); a 302 hits your server every time, so each click can be counted.
News feed fan-out on write: push each new post into followers' precomputed timelines. Reads are instant, but one celebrity post means millions of writes.
News feed hybrid: fan-out on write for normal users, fan-out on read for celebrities, merging their recent posts into the timeline at read time.
Chat system: clients hold persistent WebSocket connections, and a session service maps each user to the gateway server that holds their connection.
Chat ordering: assign per-conversation sequence numbers on the server. Client clocks drift and can't be trusted to order messages.
Chat delivery: persist the message first, then push it. Offline users catch up on reconnect by syncing everything after their last-seen sequence number.
Rate limiter design: enforce it in the API gateway or middleware, keep counters in Redis updated by atomic Lua scripts, and decide up front whether to fail open or closed.
Snowflake IDs: 64 bits = 41-bit millisecond timestamp + 10-bit machine ID + 12-bit sequence, giving roughly time-sorted unique IDs with no coordination.
Leaderboard: a Redis sorted set gives O(log n) score updates and rank lookups, ideal for top-k queries and 'what is my rank'.
Payment system: use idempotency keys end to end, a double-entry ledger, and reconciliation against the processor, since timeouts leave you unsure if a charge happened.
